steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing an SDN-based cybersecurity framework for substation communications that detects malicious GOOSE messages and localizes the attacked device. Cover background on SDN, its security problems, related mitigation work, the gap we address, our contributions, and the paper outline.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. SDN background and use in intelligent substations
- SDN: dynamic, controllable, cost-effective, flexible; emergent paradigm for high-bandwidth dynamic applications
- data traffic rising with number of intelligent electronic devices (IEDs) -> communication networks more complex
- OpenFlow-based SDN separates control and forwarding planes -> flexibility; traditional switches tightly couple them, limits scalability/functionality
- OpenFlow: first industry-standard interface between control and forwarding layers; controllers determine packet paths over switches; access to switch/router forwarding plane
- control plane manipulates forwarding -> directly program network control, abstract infrastructure for apps and services
- SDN now applied in intelligent substations: functionality, accessibility, adaptability; meets substation network demands

2. Security challenges of SDN
- security challenges hard to address
- Kreutz: seven primary possible vulnerabilities
- SDN enables dynamic flow controls, network monitoring, forensics, security policy modification, security service insertion, basic programming
- attacks on control plane communications: among most pressing issues today
- separate control/forwarding -> larger attack surface
- management at controller; controllers vulnerable to fault injection, DDoS -> significant harm
- detecting such attacks critical for future SDN deployments

3. Substation security efforts
- power vendors, researchers: reliability and security via technology, intelligent frameworks, data resources for smart substations
- priority: defend against substation cyber-attacks, e.g. intrusion detection systems (IDSs) against malicious data intrusion

4. Related SDN-based mitigation work
- plethora of SDN-based mitigation schemes
- entropy-based mitigation of DDoS on SDN control plane
- identifying/countering Slowloris (low-level DDoS) in SDN
- PIEDefender: protocol-independent component on SDN controllers vs packet injection
- Table I: recent attacks and mitigations

5. Gap and proposed approach
- many IDS efforts for control and data planes
- no work on attack localization in a substation
- GOOSE (generic object-oriented system event) messages crucial for real-time substation automation; frequent target
- this paper: rule-based IDS integrated SDN module; identifies abnormal GOOSE packets, determines fault device -> localization and response

6. Contributions
- (1) rule-based IDS-integrated SDN framework: detect malicious GOOSE, locate attacked device, disable port
- (2) validation on hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testbed, two cases: station bus SDN switch, protection IED (PIED)
- (3) time delays with/without proposed methods

7. Paper organization
- II digital substation overview; III proposed framework; IV HIL testbed; V case study performance + time delays with/without; VI conclusion, future work

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Software-defined networking (SDN) is dynamic, controllable, cost-effective and flexible, and it is an emergent paradigm that suits the high-bandwidth, dynamic applications of today. Also, data traffic is rising gradually along with the number of intelligent electronic devices (IEDs), and this makes intelligent communication networks more complex. In traditional network switches the data forwarding and data control planes are tightly coupled, which limits scalability and functionality. OpenFlow-based SDN is an advanced approach to network architecture that separates the control and forwarding planes so the network is more flexible. Using OpenFlow, SDN network controllers can determine the path network packets take over a network of switches. OpenFlow is the first industry-standard communications interface designed between the control and forwarding layers of an SDN architecture. It lets network switches and controllers access a network switch or router's forwarding plane across the network. Because the control plane can manipulate packet forwarding, the SDN architecture makes it possible to program network control directly and abstract the underlying infrastructure for applications and network services. So today SDN is applied in intelligent substations to improve the functionality, accessibility, and adaptability of communication and to meet the demands of the intelligent substation communication network.

SDN is a promising technology but it has security challenges that seem difficult to address. Kreutz's research identified seven primary possible security vulnerabilities. The literature shows that SDN allows creating dynamic flow controls, network monitoring, network forensics, security policy modification, security service insertion, and basic network programming. But attacks on control plane communications are one of the most pressing and challenging security issues even today. Having the logical control and forwarding functions separate increases the attack surface. SDN network management sits at the controller, and controllers are vulnerable to many cyber-attacks such as fault injection and distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, so this can cause significant harm. So detecting these attacks in SDN is critical for future SDN network deployments.

Power vendors and researchers are focusing on improving reliability and security through technological advancements, intelligent frameworks, and using data resources for developing smart substations. A key priority is defending against cyber-attacks on substations by implementing technologies like intrusion detection systems (IDSs) that prevent malicious data intrusion.

4. Related SDN-based mitigation work
- plethora of SDN-based mitigation schemes
- entropy-based mitigation of DDoS on SDN control plane
- identifying/countering Slowloris (low-level DDoS) in SDN
- PIEDefender: protocol-independent component on SDN controllers vs packet injection
- Table I: recent attacks and mitigations

- no work on attack localization in a substation
- GOOSE (generic object-oriented system event) messages crucial for real-time substation automation; frequent target
- this paper: rule-based IDS integrated SDN module; identifies abnormal GOOSE packets, determines fault device -> localization and response

- (1) rule-based IDS-integrated SDN framework: detect malicious GOOSE, locate attacked device, disable port
- (2) validation on hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testbed, two cases: station bus SDN switch, protection IED (PIED)
- (3) time delays with/without proposed methods

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Software-defined networking (SDN) is dynamic, controllable, cost-effective and flexible, and it is an emergent paradigm that suits the high-bandwidth, dynamic applications of today. Also, data traffic is rising gradually along with the number of intelligent electronic devices (IEDs), and this makes intelligent communication networks more complex. In traditional network switches the data forwarding and data control planes are tightly coupled, which limits scalability and functionality. OpenFlow-based SDN is an advanced approach to network architecture that separates the control and forwarding planes so the network is more flexible. Using OpenFlow, SDN network controllers can determine the path network packets take over a network of switches. OpenFlow is the first industry-standard communications interface designed between the control and forwarding layers of an SDN architecture. It lets network switches and controllers access a network switch or router's forwarding plane across the network. Because the control plane can manipulate packet forwarding, the SDN architecture makes it possible to program network control directly and abstract the underlying infrastructure for applications and network services. So today SDN is applied in intelligent substations to improve the functionality, accessibility, and adaptability of communication and to meet the demands of the intelligent substation communication network.

SDN is a promising technology but it has security challenges that seem difficult to address. Kreutz's research identified seven primary possible security vulnerabilities. The literature shows that SDN allows creating dynamic flow controls, network monitoring, network forensics, security policy modification, security service insertion, and basic network programming. But attacks on control plane communications are one of the most pressing and challenging security issues even today. Having the logical control and forwarding functions separate increases the attack surface. SDN network management sits at the controller, and controllers are vulnerable to many cyber-attacks such as fault injection and distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, so this can cause significant harm. So detecting these attacks in SDN is critical for future SDN network deployments.

Power vendors and researchers are focusing on improving reliability and security through technological advancements, intelligent frameworks, and using data resources for developing smart substations. A key priority is defending against cyber-attacks on substations by implementing technologies like intrusion detection systems (IDSs) that prevent malicious data intrusion.

There are a lot of research works in the literature on SDN-based mitigation schemes. One work proposed an entropy-based solution to mitigate DDoS attacks on the control plane of the SDN architecture. Another work gives a method for identifying and countering Slowloris, which is a low-level DDoS attack, in an SDN environment. To detect and mitigate packet injection threats, another work creates PIEDefender, which is an effective, protocol-independent component installed on SDN controllers. Table I shows a compilation of recent attacks on SDN architecture and the mitigations proposed for them.

Many similar efforts are being made to build an IDS that can identify and prevent cyber-attacks in the control and data planes of SDN architecture. But to the best of the authors' knowledge, no work has addressed attack localization in a substation. Also, generic object-oriented system event (GOOSE) messages are crucial for real-time communication in substation automation, but they are vulnerable and so they are a frequent target in cyber-attacks (as many research works mention), which shows the critical need to address their security vulnerabilities. So in this paper we introduce a rule-based IDS integrated SDN module that identifies abnormal GOOSE packets and accurately determines the fault device in the network, which helps in localizing and responding to cybersecurity threats.

The main contributions of this paper are: (1) a rule-based IDS-integrated SDN framework that detects malicious GOOSE communication, locates the attacked device, and disables the port associated with the fault, (2) validation of the proposed method on a hardware-in-the-loop (HIL)-testbed with two case scenarios, a malicious GOOSE attack on the station bus SDN switch and on the protection intelligent electronic device (PIED), (3) computing the time delays with or without the proposed methods.

The rest of the paper is organized like this: Section II gives a high-level overview of a digital substation. Section III outlines the proposed IDS-integrated SDN framework. Section IV is about the existing HIL testbed and Section V evaluates the performance of the proposed module by case study analysis. It also gives the time delays for the system configuration with and without IDS-integrated SDN. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper and gives recommendations for future work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
With its dynamic, controllable, cost-effective, and flexible nature, software-defined networking (SDN) is an emergent paradigm suitable for the high-bandwidth, dynamic applications of today. Moreover, data traffic is gradually rising along with the number of intelligent electronic devices (IEDs), making intelligent communication networks more complex. Hence, OpenFlow-based SDN is an advanced approach to network architecture that separates the control and forwarding planes to increase network flexibility, as opposed to traditional network switches, where the data forwarding and data control planes are tightly coupled, which limits scalability and functionality. SDN network controllers can determine the path taken by network packets over a network of switches using OpenFlow, the first industry-standard communications interface designed between the control and forwarding layers of an SDN architecture. It allows network switches and controllers to access a network switch or router's forwarding plane across the network. By allowing the control plane to manipulate packet forwarding, the SDN architecture makes it possible to directly program network control and abstract the underlying infrastructure for applications and network services. As a result, SDN is nowadays applied in intelligent substations to enhance the functionality, accessibility, and adaptability of communication and to meet the demands of the intelligent substation communication network.

Despite being a promising technology, SDN faces security challenges that seem difficult to address. Kreutz's research has identified seven primary possible security vulnerabilities [1]. The literature provides evidence that SDN allows for creating dynamic flow controls, network monitoring, network forensics, security policy modification, security service insertion, and basic network programming. However, attacks on control plane communications are one of the most pressing and challenging security issues that exist even today [2]. Separating the logical control and forwarding functions increases the attack surface. Since SDN network management is located at the controller, and controllers are vulnerable to various cyber-attacks, including fault injection and distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, such attacks can inflict significant harm. Thus, it is critical to detect such attacks in SDN for future SDN network deployments.

Efforts from power vendors and researchers focus on enhancing reliability and security through technological advancements, intelligent frameworks, and leveraging data resources for smart substation development. A key priority is defending against substation cyber-attacks by implementing technologies such as intrusion detection systems (IDSs) to prevent malicious data intrusion.

The literature shows a plethora of research works on SDN-based mitigation schemes. Research in [8] proposed an entropy-based solution for mitigating DDoS attacks on the control plane of the SDN architecture. The authors of [9] provide a method for identifying and countering Slowloris, a low-level DDoS attack, in an SDN environment. To detect and mitigate packet injection threats, the work in [10] creates PIEDefender, an effective, protocol-independent component installed on SDN controllers. A compilation of recent attacks on SDN architecture and their proposed mitigations is shown in Table I.

Numerous similar efforts are being made to build an IDS capable of identifying and preventing cyber-attacks in the control and data planes of SDN architecture. To the best of the authors' knowledge, though, no work has addressed attack localization in a substation. Further, generic object-oriented system event (GOOSE) messages are crucial for real-time communication in substation automation, but their vulnerability has made them a frequent target of cyber-attacks (as mentioned in many research works), emphasizing the critical need to address their security vulnerabilities. So, in this paper, a rule-based IDS [11] integrated SDN module is introduced that identifies abnormal GOOSE packets and accurately determines the fault device in the network, thus aiding in localization of and response to cybersecurity threats.

The primary contributions of this paper are: (1) a rule-based IDS-integrated SDN framework to detect malicious GOOSE communication, locate the attacked device, and disable the port associated with the fault, (2) validation of the proposed method on a hardware-in-the-loop (HIL)-testbed by implementing two case scenarios, a malicious GOOSE attack on the station bus SDN switch and on the protection intelligent electronic device (PIED), respectively, (3) computation of the time delays with or without the proposed methods.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section II presents a high-level overview of a digital substation. Section III outlines the proposed IDS-integrated SDN framework. Section IV and Section V focus on the existing HIL testbed and evaluate the performance of the proposed module by case study analysis, respectively. It also presents the time delays for the system configuration with and without IDS-integrated SDN. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper along with recommendations for future work.

References:
[1] D. Kreutz, F. M. V. Ramos, and P. Veríssimo, “Packet in message based ddos attack detection in sdn network using openflow,” in second workshop on Hot topics in software defined networking (HotSDNb12) , 2013, pp. 55–60.
[2] Z. A. Bhuiyan, S. Islam, M. M. Islam, A. B. M. A. Ullah, F. Naz, and M. S. Rahman, “On the (in)security of the control plane of sdn architecture: A survey,” IEEE Access , vol. 11, pp. 91 550–91 582, 2023.
[8] S. K. Yadav, P. Suguna, and R. L. Velusamy, “Entropy based mitigation of distributed-denial-of-service (ddos) attack on control plane in software-defined-network (sdn),” in 2019 10th International Conference on Computing, Communication and Networking Technologies (ICCCNT) , 2019, pp. 1–7.
[9] A. N. H. D. Sai, B. H. Tilak, N. S. Sanjith, P. Suhas, and R. Sanjeetha, “Detection and mitigation of low and slow ddos attack in an sdn environment,” in 2022 International Conference on Distributed Computing, VLSI, Electrical Circuits and Robotics ( DISCOVER) , 2022, pp. 106–111.
[10] J. Li, S. Qin, T. Tu, H. Zhang, and Y. Li, “Packet injection exploiting attack and mitigation in software-defined networks,” Applied Sciences , vol. 12, p. 1103, 2022.
[11] J. Hong, C.-C. Liu, and M. Govindarasu, “Integrated anomaly detection for cyber security of the substations,” IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid , vol. 5, no. 4, pp. 1643–1653, 2014.
